docs.title: TIMBER
docs.text:
TIMBER stands for Time-series Embedded Representation learning: the patches of a multichannel time series are embedded, and their representations are learned without labels. The paper develops the approach for cortical fMRI, where each channel is a cortical vertex, and shows that the representations are data-efficient, interpretable and transferable.

The package is application-agnostic. It learns from any multichannel time series given as (time, channel) arrays. The fMRI application and the paper experiments are in experiments/.

Figure: the framework of the paper. Pretraining (1) samples and patches the recordings, contextualizes the patches, encodes them and learns with the TACO task; fine-tuning (2) adds a head after the encoder.

docs.title: Why TIMBER
docs.text:
For the fMRI application of the paper:

  • Self-supervised. Pretraining needs no labels. The TACO objective predicts each patch of a channel from the patches before it, without any predefined time-position embedding.
  • Data-efficient. Pretraining uses 200 HCP subjects, and the representations are competitive with supervised baselines on gender classification and cognitive score prediction.
  • Interpretable. The attention of the encoder shows which patches each latent query reads, and integrated gradients highlight the regions behind each prediction.
  • Transferable. The same pretrained model transfers to an external clinical dataset (ABIDE I, autism detection).
  • Atlas-free. The model reads every channel (cortical vertex) directly, with no parcellation and no handcrafted connectivity measure.

docs.title: What the model does
docs.text:
1. Sampling and patching. Random channels and random time windows of a recording are cut into temporal patches.
  2. Contextualizing. The contextualizer makes the patches aware of the other channels and of their past.
  3. Encoding. The encoder summarises all the patches of an entity in a latent embedding of 512 latent queries.
  4. Task. Pretraining decoders (TACO) learn from the patches; a head predicts a target after finetuning.

docs.title: The TACO objective
docs.text:
TACO (Time-Aware COnditional reconstruction) is the pretraining task of TIMBER. Its benefits:

  • No time prior. TACO does not use a predefined time-position embedding, such as sinusoidal or rotary encodings. Such an embedding imposes a fixed assumption on the temporal structure, which can hurt the capture of brain dynamics. TACO lets the model infer the temporal relations from the data.
  • Conditioned on context. The prediction of a patch is conditioned on the contextualized patches and on the latent embedding of the whole entity, so the model learns global structure, not only the next few samples.
  • Many training samples. The task works on single patches. A run gives about 15,000 patch-level samples, which is why TIMBER learns from few subjects.
  • Better representations. The paper's ablation study shows that the TACO reconstruction task improves the prediction score on cognitive intelligence regression, compared to vanilla reconstruction.

docs.title: What the model learns
docs.text:
TIMBER produces two representations, as in the paper:

  • the latent embedding e: what the encoder returns for an entity, a compact summary of all its patches;
  • the contextualized patches z: one representation per channel and per time patch, after the contextualizer.

The latent queries (e_queries in the architecture figure) are not representations. They are the learned queries of the encoder: each one reads the contextualized patches through attention. The figure below shows the attention of three latent queries over the contextualized patches. Each query attends to a different functional network, the default mode network (A), the somatomotor network (B) and language-related regions (C), and no labels were used to learn them.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install timber-ts

The distribution is timber-ts; the import name is timber. The source is at github.com/Dubris/timber-ts. Requirements: Python 3.12 or later, PyTorch 2.15 or later, transformers 4.51.3 or later. CUDA, Apple MPS and CPU are supported.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
TIMBER turns a multichannel time series into representations in four steps. The tokenizer cuts the signal into temporal patches and embeds them; the contextualizer gives every patch its context across channels and time; the encoder summarises all the contextualized patches of an entity into a few latent embeddings; and a task module uses them: pretraining decoders during pretraining, a head during finetuning. Each module is one class of the package, and each can be resized or switched off by configuration.

Figure: (A) the four stages; (B) the contextualization and encoder modules (paper, architecture figure).

signal (entity, channel, time)
  -> tokenizer          temporal patches x_p + channel embeddings        (entity, channel, patch, patch_length)
  -> contextualizer     contextualized patches z                          (entity, channel, patch, dim)
  -> masking            hides a fraction of the patches (pretraining only)
  -> encoder            latent queries e_queries read the patches -> latent embedding e   (entity, latent, dim)
  -> decoders (pretraining)   or   head H (finetuning, plugged after the encoder)

The terms follow the paper: temporal patches x_p (the raw patches), contextualized patches z (after the contextualizer), latent queries e_queries (the learned queries of the encoder) and latent embedding e (its output). The modules are named C (contextualizer), E (encoder), D (decoders) and H (head), as in the paper.

docs.title: Shapes
docs.text:
signal has shape (*batch, channel, time). The batch axes are decomposed as follows:

  • the first batch axis is the entity: the thing that carries the label (a subject, a patient, a device). The latent embedding and the head are computed per entity;
  • the other batch axes are views of the entity, that is different samples of the same entity: recordings, channel chunks and time chunks. The head combines the views of an entity (see Finetuning heads).

A channel chunk is a random subset of the channels of a recording, and a time chunk is a window of consecutive time points. The sampler draws them at random for every sample (see Data pipeline). This is the paper's way of working with long recordings: the model sees many small random views of the same entity, which is cheap to compute and makes the representation robust to the choice of channels and of the time window.

channel indexes the channel embeddings of the tokenizer: pass channel_indices to feed a subset of them. time is the number of samples; it is cut into non-overlapping patches of patch_length samples.

docs.title: Pretraining objectives
docs.text:
TimberForPretraining runs the four steps and then the decoders listed in config.decoders. Three objectives are available, each a DecoderConfig:

  • TACO (forecasting_1, the default): the contextualized patch of each channel at time i predicts the patch that follows it, i + 1, of the same channel, with the latent embedding as context. It needs the causal mask of the contextualizer, so that the query cannot see the patch it predicts. TACO is what makes the contextualized patches informative, and it needs no explicit time-position embedding.
  • Forecasting at horizon k (forecasting_<k>): the same task, predicting the patch k steps ahead. The paper uses k = 1.
  • Vanilla reconstruction (reconstruction): the decoder predicts a masked patch from its position embedding (channel and time), without a query from the signal. This objective needs explicit time-position embeddings and a non-causal contextualizer. The ablation study of the paper shows that TACO gives better representations than this objective (see Results).

The paper also shows that adding time-position embeddings to TACO hurts the representations, so the default is TACO without them.

Patch masking (patch_mask_ratio, 0.7 in the paper) happens after the contextualizer and before the encoder: the contextualized patches of the masked positions are dropped, and the encoder only reads the others (see Encoder).

docs.title: Finetuning
docs.text: TimberForPrediction runs the same steps, then the head H is plugged after the encoder: it pools the latent embedding and predicts a regression or classification target. The paper fine-tunes the encoder and the head, and keeps the tokenizer and the contextualizer frozen (the figure of the framework shows the frozen and trainable modules). The decoders can also be trained jointly, for example with TACO as an auxiliary objective.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Every module has its own dataclass, and TimberConfig groups them. The architecture is saved in config.json; the optimisation settings are a separate object (TimberTrainingConfig) and are not saved with the model.

Dataclass Module Main fields TokenizerConfig tokenizer patch_length, patch_stride, num_channels, channel_embedding_dim ContextualizerConfig contextualizer hidden_dim, num_layers, num_heads, attention_order, is_causal EncoderConfig encoder num_latents, latent_dim, num_blocks, num_self_attention_layers, use_cls_token DecoderConfig decoders objective, loss_weight HeadConfig head task, num_outputs, pooling, fusion_stage

The configuration reference lists every field and its default. The defaults give the architecture of the experiments, except for the patch length (16 by default, 60 in the experiments) and the number of channels (set to the cortex size of the fMRI data).

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text: TimberConfig describes the architecture of a model. It is saved as config.json with the weights. Each sub-configuration is a dataclass, so unknown option names raise an error and every default is visible in the code.

docs.title: timber.configuration_timber
docs.text:
Configuration of the TIMBER models (architecture only).

TimberConfig is a PretrainedConfig: it is what config.json stores and what from_pretrained rebuilds. It is made of nested dataclasses, one per module:

  • TokenizerConfig (patching, channel and time embeddings),
  • ContextualizerConfig (paper module C),
  • EncoderConfig (paper module E; None for the no-encoder ablation),
  • a list of DecoderConfig (pretraining objectives, paper module D),
  • HeadConfig (finetuning head, paper module H; None for pretraining).

The architecture defaults are those of the TIMBER paper (TACO pretraining, forecasting_1); the data-shaped defaults (num_channels, patch_length) are placeholders to set for your data. Optimisation settings (learning rates, epochs, ...) are not part of this configuration; they belong to the training code.

Every sub-configuration validates itself in __post_init__; cross-module rules are checked by TimberConfig.validate. Unknown keys raise an error.

docs.title: Paper experiments (fMRI application)
docs.text: This folder holds the experiments of the TIMBER paper, which apply the package to cortical resting-state fMRI from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) and ABIDE. The package itself is generic: everything specific to fMRI (file names, measures, paths, configurations) lives in experiments/timber_fmri, and this folder only uses it.

docs.title: The five experiments
docs.text:
Folder Task Start from 1_learning_curve TACO pretraining on HCP, with 50 to 500 training subjects (one config per size) scratch 2_ablation_study Pretraining ablations: without TACO, causal masking, contextualizer, encoder, patch masking; one or two encoder blocks scratch 3_finetuning_hcp_intelligence Regression of the HCP cognitive scores; the tokenizer, contextualizer and first encoder block are frozen pretrained (experiment 1) 4_finetuning_hcp_gender Classification of gender on HCP pretrained 5_finetuning_abide_asd Classification of the diagnosis (DX_GROUP) on ABIDE pretrained

Each folder has the same layout:

<n>_<name>/
  train.py          # training entry point (a few lines, calls experiments.timber_fmri.training.train)
  postprocess.py    # samples the trained model over the whole dataset (embeddings, attention, predictions)
  config/
    config.yaml     # the configuration of the run (Hydra), overrides the generated groups below
    model/          # architecture (experiment 1 and 2)
    trainer/        # Lightning Trainer settings
    datamodule/     # subject splits and sampler, one file per split or size
    make_config.py  # generates the datamodule and trainer files from the cluster data

docs.title: HCP (experiments 1 to 4)
docs.text:
• One file per subject and run, stored as NumPy .npy arrays. The file name is sub-<subject>_ses-<session>_run-<run>_*.npy. The run index of the four runs of a subject is 2 * (session - 1) + (run - 1).
  • Shape: (1200, 59412), time by vertex, float32. 59412 is the fsLR 32k cortex without the medial wall. Files with the subcortex have 91282 columns (keep_subcortex: true, the default of the data module); the paper experiments use the cortex only.
  • Storage order: files stored channel by channel (Fortran order) are read much faster when training samples random channel subsets. The converter experiments/data/convert_to_channel_major.py rewrites a folder in place, safely and resumably: uv run python -m experiments.data.convert_to_channel_major --dry-run, then without --dry-run.
  • Measures: a CSV with a Subject column (the subject ids as text). Numeric measures are z-scored over the file; text measures are encoded as category codes. Subjects missing one of the used measures are dropped.
  • Complete subjects: a subject enters an experiment only if all its runs are present.

docs.title: ABIDE (experiment 5)
docs.text: • One file per subject and run, named sub-*.npy and read as (time, vertex), with the phenotypic CSV of ABIDE. The measure used is DX_GROUP.

docs.title: Atlas and assets
docs.text:
• experiments/data/ holds the assets: the spectral embedding of the cortical mesh (spectral_embeddings_64.npy), which initialises the channel embeddings, and the random parcellations (random_parcellation_*.npy) used to pool the samples. See experiments/data/description.md.
  • The Schaefer atlas (used by the analysis to report atlas regions) is read from schaefer_atlas in the paths file.

docs.title: Machine paths: paths.yaml
docs.text:
Machine-specific paths are never written in the code or in the committed configurations. They are in experiments/paths.yaml, which is git-ignored:

  1. copy experiments/paths.example.yaml to experiments/paths.yaml;
  2. set the keys for this machine (hcp_data, hcp_people, hcp_measures, abide_data, abide_measures, schaefer_atlas, results). mlruns and assets default to folders of the repository;
  3. or point the environment variable TIMBER_PATHS to another file.

In Python, use from experiments.timber_fmri.paths import PATHS and then PATHS.hcp_data. In the YAML configurations, use ${path:hcp_data}, also inside a string (${path:mlruns}/<experiment>/<run>/checkpoints/last.ckpt). Relative paths are relative to the repository root.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The configuration of a run is config/config.yaml. It lists its groups (model, trainer, datamodule) and then its own values, which override the groups. The sections are:

Section Content name_experiment, name_run, seed MLflow experiment and run names, random seed pretrained a Hugging Face folder, or a Lightning checkpoint of these modules, to start from resume_from a Lightning checkpoint to resume (the MLflow run id is read from its path) freeze / discard parameter prefixes to freeze, and pretrained parameters not to load channel_embedding_init initial channel embeddings, when training from scratch model the TimberConfig; with pretrained, only the changes from the pretrained configuration training the TimberTrainingConfig (learning rates, epochs, ...) datamodule the subjects, the sampler and the loader (see docs/data.md) trainer arguments of the Lightning Trainer callbacks checkpoints, early stopping, periodic checkpoints

The generated files of datamodule/ and trainer/ are created by config/make_config.py, which needs the cluster data. They are git-ignored, so generate them on each machine.

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
From the repository root:

uv run python -m experiments.1_learning_curve.train
uv run python -m experiments.1_learning_curve.train training.max_epochs=2 datamodule.num_workers=4   # overrides
  • The run is logged to MLflow in mlruns (${path:mlruns}). List the runs with uv run python -m experiments.timber_fmri.tracking, or open mlflow ui --backend-store-uri experiments/mlruns.
  • Checkpoints are written to <run>/checkpoints/. The callbacks.checkpoint section chooses what is kept (for example the best one by val/loss, and optionally the last one).
  • The data loader can read the files with several threads per worker (datamodule.read_threads), which helps on slow drives; 0 uses the memory map.

Experiment 2 has seven ablation configurations, config/config_1.yaml to config_7.yaml. Each is a complete configuration; select one with --config-name:

uv run python -m experiments.2_ablation_study.train --config-name config_4

docs.title: Post-processing
docs.text:
postprocess.py loads a checkpoint, runs it over every subject of the dataset without masking, and saves the results as an xarray dataset (a pickle):

uv run python -m experiments.1_learning_curve.postprocess --path_ckpt <checkpoint.ckpt> [--path_save <file.pkl>]

The results have one entry per subject and run, and per latent or channel (optionally averaged over the regions of an atlas). They are read by the notebooks of the paper. docs/data.md describes how the batches are built. analysis.py documents what is sampled: the contextualised patches, the latents of each block with their attention, and the predictions and pooled latents of a finetuned head.

docs.title: Modules of experiments/timber_fmri
docs.text: Module Purpose data.py The fMRI data: file names, measures, FmriDataset and FmriDataModule (subjects are mapped to entities, runs to recordings, vertices to channels). paths.py PATHS: the machine paths of paths.yaml, and the ${path:...} resolver of the YAML files. presets.py paper_config(): the architecture and sampler of the paper; spectral_embeddings_path(). training.py train(cfg): builds the model, the data module, the logger and the callbacks, then fits. Used by every train.py. loading.py Loads a configuration, a model or pretrained weights from a Hugging Face folder or a Lightning checkpoint; lists the subjects of a pretraining run. analysis.py model_outputs (one forward pass returning an Activations object) and sample_model / sample_model_finetuning (the post-processing). callbacks.py PlateauRelativeEarlyStopping: stops when the relative improvement over a window of validations is small. configs.py deep_merge and deep_diff for configurations, and split_subjects for the subject lists. tracking.py Lists the MLflow runs of a folder without a server. tests/ Tests of the application: file names, measures, paths, callbacks, and smoke runs of pretraining, finetuning and analysis on synthetic data.

docs.title: Settings of the experiments
docs.text:
Experiment 1 uses the pretraining setting of the paper. The values are those of its configuration:

Setting Value Patch length, channels per chunk, window 60 samples, 1024 channels, 900 samples (the 1200-sample runs are cropped by 300) Contextualizer: width, layers, heads, feed-forward ratio 128, 3, 4, 2 Encoder: latents, latent width, blocks, self-attention layers 512, 256, 2, 4 Decoder TACO (forecasting_1), widening factor 1 Patch masking ratio 0.7 Learning rate, weight decay, epochs 2e-4, 0.01, 30 (no gradient clipping) Batch chunks_per_batch 2, 2, 2, 1: 8 runs (2 subjects, 2 runs, 2 channel sets)

Experiments 3 to 5 start from the pretrained model and train a head. They freeze the tokenizer, the contextualizer, the first encoder block and the latent queries (freeze), and they use mean pooling. The exact values of each experiment are in its config/config.yaml.

Points worth knowing when reading the results:

  • Masking. Each row of a batch hides exactly floor(patch_mask_ratio * number of patches) patches, which keeps the tensors of a fixed shape (see docs/modules/encoder.md).
  • Channel embedding. The fMRI experiments start the channel embedding from a spectral embedding of the cortical mesh (channel_embedding_init), and training refines it.
  • Vertices. The fsLR 32k cortex has 59,412 vertices without the medial wall (NUM_CORTICAL_VERTICES).
  • Probes and saliency. The ridge probes are in experiments/postprocessing.ipynb; the integrated-gradient maps are in experiments/exploration.ipynb. The package provides the embeddings, the attention weights and the pooled latents (experiments/timber_fmri/analysis.py) that these analyses use.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
uv run --no-sync pytest experiments/timber_fmri

The tests use synthetic data. One of them checks that every path used in the configurations and scripts is documented in paths.example.yaml.

docs.title: Model reference
docs.text: The models are Hugging Face PreTrainedModels. TimberModel is the backbone that produces the embeddings; the two task models add the pretraining decoders or the finetuning head around it. Their forward methods return the typed output objects listed below.

docs.title: timber.modeling_timber
docs.text:
TIMBER models as Hugging Face PreTrainedModel.

  • TimberModel: tokenizer -> contextualizer -> Perceiver encoder; returns the latents (the embeddings) and the intermediate tensors.
  • TimberForPretraining: TimberModel + the decoders of config.decoders (TACO forecasting, reconstruction); computes the pretraining loss.
  • TimberForPrediction: TimberModel + a regression or classification head (config.head), optionally with pretraining decoders trained jointly (e.g. TACO finetuning).

Inputs follow the data loader layout: signal is (*batch, channel, time). The leading batch axis is the entity axis: signal.shape[0] entities, each with prod(batch[1:]) views (recordings, channel chunks, time chunks), flattened entity-major.

Example::

model = TimberModel.from_pretrained("path/or/hub-id")
embeddings = model(signal, channel_indices=channels, mask_patches=False).last_hidden_state

docs.title: TimberModel
docs.text:
Bases: TimberPreTrainedModel

Tokenizer, contextualizer and Perceiver encoder: multichannel signal -> latent embeddings.

Parameters:

docs.title: Attention
docs.text:
All attention goes through torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention, so the fused kernels of CUDA and Apple MPS are used when they apply. The three shared blocks are:

  • MultiHeadAttention: the attention itself, with boolean masks (True means "may attend");
  • FeedForward: the position-wise MLP after each attention;
  • PerceiverLayer: cross-attention from queries to a context, then a feed-forward block. The encoder and decoders are built from it.

On MPS the explicit attention path is used whenever gradients or dropout are active: the fused kernel rejects dropout, and the explicit path has faster backward passes there.

docs.title: Contextualizer
docs.text: The contextualizer (paper module C) lets the signal content of each patch flow across the other channels and over time, into the past of its own channel. A patch on its own is a short window of one channel; after the contextualizer, it carries the state of the other channels at that moment and the history of its channel, which is what captures the spatio-temporal structure of the recording. Its output, the contextualized patches z, is the input of the encoder and of the TACO decoder.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
The contextualizer factorises the attention over the two dimensions of the patch grid (channel, patch). Each of its num_layers layers (3 in the paper) runs:

  • an attention over channels at each patch time: all the channels attend to each other, at a given time;
  • a attention over time for each channel: the patches of a channel attend along time, and with is_causal=True a patch only sees the patches before it;

followed by a feed-forward block. Factorising the two passes, instead of attending over every pair of patches, reduces the cost of the attention from O(N_c^2 N_t^2) to O(N_t N_c^2 + N_c N_t^2): with the paper's sizes (1,024 channels, 15 patches) it is about a 15-fold speed-up. The two passes use the same attention parameters by default (share_attention_weights=True) and run in the order attention_order ("channel_time": channels first, as in the paper).

docs.title: The inputs
docs.text:
Each patch enters the contextualizer as two projections that are summed: a projection of the signal of the patch (patch_length samples to hidden_dim) and a projection of its position. The position is the channel embedding, and, when a time embedding is configured, the time embedding too (see Tokenizer). The two projections are summed rather than concatenated, so that masked patches can drop their whole signal term, bias included.

Whether the position includes time depends on the objective:

  • for TACO, as in the paper, the position is the channel embedding only: the temporal order is inferred from the causal attention, and no time-position embedding is given;
  • for the vanilla reconstruction objective, the paper adds sinusoidal time-position embeddings, and removes the causal mask, since the time order is then given explicitly.

Each patch is embedded as signal_projection(signal) + position_projection(position) (position = channel and time embeddings concatenated), then every layer attends over the channel axis at each patch time and over the patch (time) axis at each channel, followed by a feed-forward block. The pass over time can be causal, so that a contextualised patch only depends on the past (needed for the TACO forecasting objective).

docs.title: Decoders and pretraining objectives
docs.text:
The decoders (paper module D) are the pretraining heads. They read the latent embedding and predict patches of the signal; the loss compares each prediction with the true patch. A decoder does not reconstruct a whole recording: it predicts one patch at a time, chosen by a query. Like the encoder, a decoder is a Perceiver IO cross-attention layer (Jaegle et al., 2022).

Two objectives are used in the paper: the vanilla patch reconstruction task, and the TACO reconstruction task. The first predicts a masked patch from its position in the recording; the second predicts the next patch of a channel from the contextualized patches. The rest of this page focuses on TACO, the objective of the paper. TACO does not use a predefined time-position embedding (sinusoidal, rotary or other): such an embedding imposes a prior on the temporal structure, which can hurt the capture of the dynamics. The objective lets the model infer the temporal relations from the data.

docs.title: TACO: Time-Aware Conditional reconstruction
docs.text:
The paper's objective is TACO. For a node v and a patch time i, the query is the contextualised patch z of the previous time step, and the decoder predicts the patch x at time i, conditioned on the latents e:

x_hat(v, i) = CA(query = z(v, i-1), key/value = e)     loss = MSE(x_hat, x)  over all nodes and patch times

The figure below shows the task as the paper draws it: the contextualised patch at time t_i queries the latents and predicts the patch at t_(i+1) (paper, architecture figure, panel A, stage 4).

Because the query is a contextualised patch, the prediction can use the global context of the contextualizer and the latents, but not the patch it predicts, which the causal mask of the contextualizer keeps from the query. In the code this is the objective forecasting_1: the query is a contextualised patch and the target is the patch k steps later. TACO therefore needs no explicit time-position encoding. The paper's ablations show this matters: adding sinusoidal time encodings lowers the representation quality.

docs.title: How a decoder works
docs.text:
A decoder is a cross-attention layer: its queries attend to the latents, and the result is projected to one patch of patch_length samples. The objectives differ only in what the queries and targets are:

  • Forecasting (forecasting_<k>; TACO is forecasting_1): query = contextualised patch, target = the patch k steps later in the same channel.
  • Reconstruction (reconstruction): query = the position embeddings of the target patch, target = its raw signal. The paper uses this objective with time-position encodings as an ablation (configuration 1); it is not the default.

The loss is the mean squared error between predicted and target patches, weighted by loss_weight. Several decoders can be combined, with one DecoderConfig each.

  • Reconstruction: the queries are the position embeddings of the masked patches and the targets are their raw signal.

docs.title: Encoder
docs.text: The encoder (paper module E) compresses the contextualised patches of an entity into a fixed number of latent embedding e: 512 latent vectors of dimension 256 in the paper, whatever the number of channels. The design follows Perceiver IO (Jaegle et al., 2022): a small set of learned latent queries e_queries reads the (large) input through cross-attention, then refines itself.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
1. Cross-attention. The latent queries attend to the contextualized patches (keys and values), so that each query gathers the information it needs from the whole recording.
  2. Latent self-attention. num_self_attention_layers layers let the latents exchange information.
  3. Blocks. The cross-attention and self-attention are repeated num_blocks times. Each block re-attends the refined latents to the same patches. The latents of every block are kept, because the paper's analyses read several of them.

An optional CLS token is appended to the latents (use_cls_token); the head uses it when pooling is "cls_token".

docs.title: Patch masking
docs.text:
During pretraining, a fraction patch_mask_ratio (0.7 in the paper) of the contextualized patches is hidden from the encoder. The masking takes place after the contextualizer and before the encoder: the contextualizer sees the whole recording, and the encoder only reads the patches that are not masked. The model must then infer the hidden content from the rest instead of copying its input.

The paper draws each patch independently with a Bernoulli(patch_mask_ratio) trial. The implementation hides exactly floor(patch_mask_ratio * number of patches) patches in every row of the batch, so that the kept patches form a tensor of static shape (efficient on MPS and with torch.compile). The expected fraction is the same. The encoder selects the kept patches before the cross-attention, so keys and values are only computed for them.

docs.title: Finetuning heads
docs.text: The head (paper module H) turns the latents of an entity into a prediction: a regression vector or class logits. It is what changes between tasks. The paper's method pools the latents with attention and applies a small MLP; the fMRI experiments use mean pooling (see the table below).

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
The head reads the latent embedding e of each view and predicts the target. It has three stages:

  • Pooling summarises the latent queries of a view into one vector:
  • "attention" (the paper's method): a softmax over a learned linear score of each latent query, so that the queries that matter most for the target get the largest weights; the weights are returned for inspection;
  • "mean": the average of the latent queries (the fMRI experiments);
  • "weighted_mean": a softmax-weighted average with one learned weight per latent query;
  • "cls_token": the last token, which needs use_cls_token=True in the encoder. An optional Linear + GELU projection (projection_dim) and input dropout (pooling_input_dropout) apply to every token before pooling.
  • View fusion combines the views of an entity (recordings, channel chunks, time chunks). fusion_stage decides where: "early" averages the pooled views before the MLP, so there is one prediction per entity; "late" predicts for each view and averages the predictions; "loss" keeps one prediction per view and computes the loss on each, with the entity's label repeated.
  • MLP maps the fused vector to num_outputs values, through num_hidden_layers hidden layers (0 in the experiments: a single linear layer) with dropout.

The loss depends on the task. Regression uses the Huber loss, as in the paper. Classification uses cross-entropy, with label_smoothing (0.05 in experiment 4).

An entity contributes several views (recordings, channel chunks, time chunks) to a batch. fusion_stage sets where the views of an entity are combined:

  • "early": average the pooled latents of the views, then apply the MLP once per entity;
  • "late": apply the MLP per view, then average the predictions (fuse_views);
  • "loss": keep one prediction per view and repeat the entity label for each view.

docs.title: Tokenizer
docs.text: The tokenizer turns a raw multichannel recording into patch embeddings, one per channel and patch. It is the only place where the input samples enter the model, and where the model learns what each channel is.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
1. Patching. Each channel is cut into non-overlapping patches of patch_length samples (60 in the paper, so 15 patches for a window of 900 samples). patch_stride gives overlapping patches; None means non-overlapping.
  2. Channel embedding. Each channel has a vector of size channel_embedding_dim (64 in the paper), which tells the model which node a patch comes from. In the paper it is learned. The fMRI experiments start it from a spectral embedding of the cortical mesh (channel_embedding_init), which training then refines.
  3. Output. The tokenizer returns a TokenizerOutput with the patches, the channel embeddings and, if enabled, the time embeddings. The next modules read it (see Contextualizer).
  4. Time embedding (optional). time_embedding_type adds a Fourier embedding of the time. The paper's pretraining uses none: the time order is inferred from the causal attention. The option exists for the time-encoding ablation, with "patch" (the patch index) or "timestep" (the absolute timestep of the patch start).

docs.title: Data pipeline
docs.text:
timber.data turns time-series recordings into the batches the model is trained on. The examples of this section, like the rest of the Training part, follow the fMRI application of the paper: each entity is a subject, each recording a run, and each channel a cortical vertex.

files  ->  NpyTimeSeriesDataset  ->  PartitionSampler  ->  TimberDataModule  ->  batches
(arrays)   (reads a window)         (draws the grid)      (splits the entities)  (signal, positions, labels)

docs.title: Input files
docs.text:
Each file is one recording of one entity, stored as a NumPy .npy array of shape (time, channel), typically float32. You describe the files with a mapping from keys to paths:

files = {
    ("subject-01", 0): "data/subject-01_run-0.npy",   # (entity, recording)
    ("subject-01", 1): "data/subject-01_run-1.npy",
    ("subject-02", 0): "data/subject-02_run-0.npy",
}

Storage order. Random channel subsets read much faster from files stored channel by channel, that is in Fortran order. Save such files with np.save(path, np.asfortranarray(array)): the shape stays (time, channel), and both orders are read correctly. The fMRI experiments include a converter for existing folders (experiments/data/convert_to_channel_major.py).

docs.title: Sampling: a random grid of chunks
docs.text:
The paper never feeds a whole recording to the model. Each recording has about 60,000 channels and 1,200 time points, and attention over all of them is out of reach. Instead, every training sample is a random sub-grid of the data:

  • Channels: a random subset of 1,024 of the 59,412 cortical vertices (node sampling), so that the attention runs over 1,024 channels;
  • Time: a random window of 900 of the 1,200 time points (the window is contiguous, so that the temporal attention sees a real time course).

Sampling is a computational necessity, and it also helps learning. The paper argues that nearby and functionally related vertices are highly correlated, so a subset preserves the dominant spatiotemporal patterns: each draw is a noisy view of the same recording. The model sees a different view at every step, which reduces overfitting and makes it more robust to spatial and temporal perturbations (see the paper's sampling and patching section).

The sampler works on a grid with one axis per dimension: entities, recordings, channels, time and, optionally, shards. Along each axis it cuts the indices into chunks of chunk_shape consecutive elements, and a batch takes chunks_per_batch chunks along every axis. Each combination of chunks is one sample:

  • a channel chunk is a set of channels of one recording (for example 32 of the 1,024 sampled channels);
  • a time chunk is a window of consecutive time points (for example 128 samples of a 900-sample window).

The steps, in order: shuffle each axis if asked (shuffle_before_chunking), cut it into chunks, optionally stratify the chunks by label (labels: one element of every label per chunk), pad the axis to a multiple of the batch size, group the chunks into batches, and crop each chunk randomly (crop_shape, for example to take 900 of 1,200 samples).

Setting Meaning partition_shape Size of every axis: (entities, recordings, channels, time). chunk_shape Elements per chunk along each axis. The paper: (1, 1, 1024, 900) for one entity, one recording, 1,024 channels and a 900-sample window. chunks_per_batch Chunks per batch along each axis; the batch holds the product of these. shuffle_before_chunking Shuffle each axis before cutting it into chunks. Set it to False for time, otherwise a chunk of time points is spread over the recording instead of forming a window. crop_shape Elements randomly cropped from each chunk. The paper crops 1,200 samples to 900 with (0, 0, 0, 300). labels Stratify an axis by label, so that each chunk holds every class. resample_per_batch Redraw the indices of every batch along the chosen axes. seed Base seed; the batches of an epoch depend only on seed and the epoch number.

The paper's batch of 8 runs is chunks_per_batch = (2, 2, 2, 1): 2 subjects, 2 runs, 2 channel chunks of 1,024 vertices, one time window. ChunkCollator reshapes the samples back to (*chunks_per_batch, channel, time).

sampler = {
    "partition_shape": [100, 2, 59412, 1200],
    "chunk_shape": [1, 1, 1024, 900],                       # 1,024 random vertices, a 900-sample window
    "chunks_per_batch": [2, 2, 2, 1],
    "shuffle_before_chunking": [True, True, True, False],   # time windows stay contiguous
    "crop_shape": [0, 0, 0, 300],                           # 1,200 samples -> random 900-sample window
}

docs.title: Shards
docs.text:
A shard is a file that holds a subset of the channels of a recording. A recording stored as several shards is one recording split by channel: the files subject-01_run-0_shard-0.npy and subject-01_run-0_shard-1.npy could hold the first and the second half of the vertices. The key of a shard is (entity, recording, shard), and channel_index maps the local channels of each shard to the global channel indices, so that the model still knows which vertex is which.

In the fMRI application, a shard is a set of cortical vertices of a recording. The paper draws 1,024 random vertices out of about 60,000 for every sample; storing the recording split by vertex subsets gives the same channel split on disk. The package reads any number of shards per recording. To sample across shards, add the shard count as a fifth axis of partition_shape (see the example in Usage); with four axes the sampler always reads shard 0.

files = {
    ("subject-01", 0, 0): "data/subject-01_run-0_shard-0.npy",  # vertices 0 to 31 of the cortex
    ("subject-01", 0, 1): "data/subject-01_run-0_shard-1.npy",  # vertices 32 to 63
    ("subject-02", 0, 0): "data/subject-02_run-0_shard-0.npy",
    ("subject-02", 0, 1): "data/subject-02_run-0_shard-1.npy",
}
channel_index = {0: np.arange(0, 32), 1: np.arange(32, 64)}   # local channel -> global vertex, per shard

docs.title: Preprocessing the paper applies
docs.text:
The package does not preprocess the signals; the model expects them preprocessed as in the paper:

  • HCP (S1200, resting state): the HCP minimal preprocessing pipeline (motion correction, spatial normalisation to MNI space, ICA-FIX denoising), a band-pass filter of 0.01–0.1 Hz, and a z-score per vertex. The paper uses 948 subjects with complete data (four runs of 1,200 time points, TR = 0.72 s) and pretrains on 200 of them. The cortex has 59,412 vertices without the medial wall (fsLR 32k).
  • ABIDE I: 871 subjects (403 ASD, 468 controls), processed with C-PAC (motion correction, normalisation, nuisance regression). Each run is resampled to TR = 0.72 s and brought to 1,200 time points by repeating it, then band-pass filtered and z-scored per vertex, as for HCP.

docs.title: Datasets and data modules
docs.text:
• NpyTimeSeriesDataset reads one window per index. Its load(path) method can be overridden to read another storage layout. It can also resample the time window and the channels at random, deterministically for each index and epoch.
  • TimberDataModule splits the entities into train, validation and test sets (by number, or by explicit lists) and builds one data loader per split. It is configured with DataModuleConfig.
  • Batches are tuples (signal, positions, labels): signal is the float32 (view..., channel, time) tensor, positions a SamplePositions with the entity, recording, channel and timestep of every sample, and labels the targets of the entities, or None.

Every option and its default is in the reference below.

docs.title: timber.data.sampler
docs.text:
Sampler that cuts an (entity, recording, channel, time) data grid into chunks and batches.

The data is a grid with one axis per dimension: entities (what carries the labels: a subject, a patient, a machine), recordings of an entity, channels, timepoints, and optionally shards (a recording stored as several channel-subset files). Along each axis the indices are (optionally) shuffled and cut into chunks of chunk_shape[axis] consecutive elements. A batch takes chunks_per_batch[axis] chunks along every axis, and the sampler yields one index tuple per combination (the Cartesian product of the chunks), so a batch has prod(chunks_per_batch) samples. ChunkCollator reshapes it back to (*chunks_per_batch, channel, time).

Example: partition_shape = (entities, 4 recordings, 10000 channels, 1200 timepoints), chunk_shape = (1, 1, 1024, 1200), chunks_per_batch = (2, 2, 2, 1): each batch has 2 entities x 2 recordings x 2 sets of 1024 channels x 1 window of 1200 timepoints (cropped to 900 with crop_shape = (0, 0, 0, 300)).

The batches of an epoch depend only on seed + epoch (call set_epoch).

docs.text:

A recording may be split into several shards (channel-subset files); channel_index then maps the local channel indices of every shard to global channel indices.

Files are memory-mapped: the OS page cache is shared by the DataLoader workers, so the data is not duplicated per worker. Override NpyTimeSeriesDataset.load to read another storage layout.

Storage order: a random subset of channels is read much faster from a file stored channel by channel. Save such files in Fortran order (np.save(path, np.asfortranarray(series)); the array keeps its (time, channel) shape, the .npy header records the order): a chunk then reads one contiguous run per channel instead of scattered bytes of every time row (about 50x less I/O for 1024 of 60k channels). Both orders are read transparently.

Threaded reads: on drives with a high latency (USB SSDs, network file systems), a memory map reads one page at a time per process. With read_threads > 0, the channels of channel-major files are read with concurrent os.pread calls instead (they release the GIL), which keeps many requests in flight (about 7x faster per process on a USB SSD). The items are identical.

docs.title: Training with Lightning
docs.text: timber.lightning wraps the Hugging Face models in PyTorch Lightning modules. The wrappers add the training loop, the optimiser and schedule, the metrics, and the loading and export of weights. The model itself stays a plain transformers model, so you can always take it out with module.model.

docs.title: The modules
docs.text:
Class Wraps Use it to TimberPretrainingModule TimberForPretraining learn the representation with the pretraining objectives TimberFinetuningModule TimberForPrediction train a head, optionally with pretraining decoders

Both take the model configuration, the optimisation settings and, when training from scratch, the initial channel embeddings:

from timber.lightning import TimberFinetuningModule, TimberPretrainingModule

module = TimberPretrainingModule(
    config,                                   # TimberConfig: the architecture
    training={"learning_rate": 1e-4, "max_epochs": 30},  # TimberTrainingConfig fields
    channel_embedding_init=None,              # or an array of shape (num_channels, channel_embedding_dim)
)

docs.title: Optimisation
docs.text:
TimberTrainingConfig holds the optimisation settings. It is not saved with the model; it is kept in the Lightning checkpoint.

Field Default Meaning learning_rate 1e-4 AdamW learning rate of the backbone. weight_decay 1e-2 AdamW weight decay; biases and norm weights are not decayed. head_learning_rate None Learning rate of the head, if different. latents_learning_rate None Learning rate of the latents, if different. warmup_ratio 0.1 Fraction of the steps with a linear warm-up, then a cosine decay. max_epochs 30 Number of epochs. grad_norm_log_interval 50 How often the gradient norm is logged, in steps. compile False Compile the attention layers with torch.compile.

Gradient clipping is set on the trainer (gradient_clip_val). Lightning refuses to clip the gradients of a fused optimiser under mixed precision, so the optimiser is not fused when clipping is on.

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
from lightning.pytorch import Trainer
from timber.device import default_precision

trainer = Trainer(max_epochs=30, precision=default_precision(), gradient_clip_val=5.0)
trainer.fit(module, datamodule=datamodule)

The default precision is bf16-mixed on CUDA and MPS and 32-true on CPU. Losses and metrics are computed in float32.

docs.title: Finetuning
docs.text:
TimberFinetuningModule can start from a pretrained backbone, from a Hugging Face folder or a Hub id, or from a Lightning checkpoint of these modules:

module = TimberFinetuningModule(finetune_config, training={"learning_rate": 2e-5, "head_learning_rate": 2e-4})
module.load_pretrained("my-timber")                  # a Hugging Face folder or Hub id
module.freeze_parameters(["timber.tokenizer", "timber.contextualizer", "timber.encoder.blocks.0"])
  • load_pretrained(source, discard=(...)) loads the weights that match. discard lists the prefixes not to load, such as the pretraining decoders, which a finetuning model does not have.
  • freeze_parameters(patterns) freezes the parameters whose names start with a pattern. Frozen modules are kept in eval() mode during training, so their dropout is off and they run without autograd when the whole front end is frozen.

The folder loads back with TimberModel.from_pretrained("my-timber") (or TimberForPrediction, TimberForPretraining for the other tasks), and with AutoModel.from_pretrained after import timber.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: The results below are those of the paper (Le Bris, Barbano and Wassermann, under review, hal.science/hal-05632181). The numbers are quoted, not recomputed here. The Paper experiments page describes how to rerun the experiments, and the paper has the full tables and the statistical tests.

docs.title: Representations from 200 subjects
docs.text:
Pretrained on 200 HCP subjects (800 runs) without labels, TIMBER gives representations that are competitive with or better than supervised baselines on gender classification and cognitive intelligence score prediction, whether those baselines are trained end-to-end or fine-tuned after large-scale pretraining. Two kinds of representation are evaluated with ridge probes:

  • the contextualised patches z, averaged over the runs and pooled into the Schaefer 800-parcel atlas;
  • the latent embedding e (512 latents of dimension 256), which needs no atlas.

For intelligence scores, the paper reports that TIMBER outperforms the FC-based and voxel-based baselines in MSE and MAE, and that the patches and the latents are significantly better than the FC matrix baseline.

docs.title: Fine-tuning
docs.text: Fine-tuning the encoder with an MLP head improves the latent embedding only slightly on HCP, and not to a statistically significant degree in the paper's tests. The head is kept for interpretability: it gives the attention weights and saliency maps used below.

docs.title: Generalisation to ABIDE I
docs.text: Without any fine-tuning, the pretrained latents classify autism (ASD versus controls) with 65.0 % accuracy in stratified 10-fold cross-validation with site-wise and condition-wise splits. Fine-tuning raises the accuracy to 68.9 %. The best published ensembles reach 75.2 % on the same protocol (paper, table of the ABIDE experiment), so TIMBER is not state of the art on this task.

docs.title: Data efficiency
docs.text:
Learning curves on HCP (paper, learning-curve figure of the appendix): the training set grows from 50 to 500 subjects; test on 400 unseen subjects, 10-fold cross-validation, 95 % confidence bands.

The patch representations plateau at about 100 training subjects. The latent embeddings peak at 200 and then decline: the paper attributes this to the encoder over-optimising the pretraining task as the data and the number of steps grow, which is why fine-tuning the encoder is recommended for larger training sets.

docs.title: Ablation study
docs.text:
The paper removes one component at a time (configurations 1 to 5 of the experiments), and measures the PCC of the cognitive score prediction:

Configuration Latents e (PCC) Patches z (PCC) Reading Full model 0.388 0.378 reference 1. Standard reconstruction (no TACO) 0.303 0.045 TACO matters most for the patches 2. Time-position encodings instead of causal masking 0.199 0.242 explicit time encodings hurt 3. No contextualizer 0.055 n/a the contextualizer is essential for the latents 4. No encoder n/a 0.033 the encoder is essential for the patches 5. No patch masking 0.196 0.175 masking helps both

The paper's conclusion: the contextualizer and the encoder are complementary, the TACO objective is what makes the contextualised patches informative, and explicit time encodings are unnecessary. Values are the PCC of the cognitive score prediction (paper, ablation table).

docs.title: Interpretability
docs.text:
The architecture exposes two views of what the model uses.

Attention maps. The cross-attention of the first encoder block shows which patches each latent reads. Three latents of the paper attend to the default mode network, the somatomotor network and language-related regions.

Attention of three latent queries to the contextualised patches (paper, attention figure).

Integrated gradients. For each target, the paper attributes the prediction to the contextualised patches with integrated gradients (Sundararajan et al., 2017), then averages the attributions over time and maps them to the cortex. For cognitive intelligence the importance is concentrated in the left hemisphere, in language-related areas; the paper also shows the maps for gender and for ASD detection.

Integrated-gradient attribution maps for cognitive intelligence (A), gender (B) and ASD detection (C) (paper, integrated-gradient figure).

The repository exposes what these analyses need: the attention weights of the encoder and the pooled latents of the head (experiments/timber_fmri/analysis.py). The integrated-gradient maps are computed in experiments/exploration.ipynb, and the ridge probes in experiments/postprocessing.ipynb.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: The examples of this page use the same small model as the README, so that they run on a laptop. Real settings are in the configuration reference and in the paper.

docs.title: Build a model
docs.text:
A TIMBER model is described by a TimberConfig, made of one sub-configuration per module. Any field you leave out takes the default of the paper's pretraining setting. The arguments of each module are:

  • tokenizer: patch length, number of channels, channel embedding size (TokenizerConfig);
  • contextualizer: width, number of layers, heads, causal or not (ContextualizerConfig);
  • encoder: number of latent queries and their width, number of blocks (EncoderConfig);
  • decoders: one entry per pretraining objective, such as TACO (DecoderConfig);
  • head: for finetuning only (HeadConfig).
import torch
from timber import TimberConfig, TimberForPretraining

config = TimberConfig(
    tokenizer={"patch_length": 16, "num_channels": 64, "channel_embedding_dim": 64},
    contextualizer={
        "hidden_dim": 128,        # width of the contextualizer layers
        "num_layers": 3,          # alternating channel and time attention layers
        "num_heads": 4,
        "is_causal": True,        # a patch only sees the past along time (required by TACO)
    },
    encoder={
        "num_latents": 32,        # latent queries, the summary of an entity
        "latent_dim": 256,
        "num_blocks": 2,
    },
    decoders=[{"objective": "forecasting_1"}],  # TACO: predict the next patch of each channel
    patch_mask_ratio=0.7,                         # hide 70% of the patches before the encoder
)
model = TimberForPretraining(config)
output = model(torch.randn(4, 64, 128))  # (entity, channel, time)
output.loss.backward()

docs.title: Get representations for downstream tasks
docs.text:
The backbone, TimberModel, returns two representations, both without masking:

  • the latent embedding (last_hidden_state, (entity, latent, latent_dim)): a compact summary of all the patches of an entity, used by linear probes and finetuning heads;
  • the contextualized patches (contextualized, (entity, channel, patch, dim)): one representation per channel and per time patch, before the encoder.
from timber import TimberModel

model.save_pretrained("my-timber")
backbone = TimberModel.from_pretrained("my-timber").eval()
with torch.inference_mode():
    out = backbone(torch.randn(4, 64, 128), mask_patches=False)
latent_embedding = out.last_hidden_state   # (4, 33, 256): 32 latent queries + 1 CLS token, if enabled
patches = out.contextualized                # (4, 64, 8, 128): 8 patches of 16 samples per channel

To embed a subset of the channels, pass channel_indices as explained in the README.

For a whole dataset, the data pipeline gives the batches. Here the recordings are split into two channel shards, and each training sample takes a random 128-sample time window:

import numpy as np
from timber import TimberConfig
from timber.data import TimberDataModule

files = {  # (entity, recording, shard) -> (time, channel) array of the shard
    ("subject-01", 0, 0): "subject-01_run-0_shard-0.npy", ("subject-01", 0, 1): "subject-01_run-0_shard-1.npy",
    ("subject-02", 0, 0): "subject-02_run-0_shard-0.npy", ("subject-02", 0, 1): "subject-02_run-0_shard-1.npy",
}
channel_index = {0: np.arange(0, 8), 1: np.arange(8, 16)}  # channels of each shard -> global channels
datamodule = TimberDataModule(
    {
        "sampler": {
            "partition_shape": [2, 1, 8, 300, 2],        # entities, recordings, channels per shard, time, shards
            "chunk_shape": [1, 1, 4, 128, 1],            # 4 channels and a 128-sample window per chunk
            "chunks_per_batch": [2, 1, 1, 1, 1],         # 2 entities per batch, one chunk along each other axis
            "shuffle_before_chunking": [True, True, True, False, True],  # the time window is contiguous
        },
        "num_train_entities": 2, "num_val_entities": 0, "num_test_entities": 0,
        "resample_time_window": True,                   # a new random window at every epoch
    },
    files,
    channel_index=channel_index,
)
datamodule.setup()
signal, positions, _ = next(iter(datamodule.train_dataloader()))
# signal: (2, 1, 1, 1, 4, 128): the shard axis is merged into the channel-chunk axis, each chunk comes from one shard

docs.title: Finetune
docs.text:
Finetuning uses a model with a head and no pretraining decoder, loaded from the pretrained backbone. The head is plugged after the encoder; the backbone parameters keep their pretrained values and can be frozen:

from timber import TimberForPrediction

model = TimberForPrediction.from_pretrained(
    "my-timber",
    head={"task": "classification", "num_outputs": 2},  # the head, after the encoder
    decoders=[],                                          # drop the pretraining decoder
    patch_mask_ratio=0.0,                                 # no masking at finetuning time
)

For a training loop with labels, see Training with Lightning.

docs.title: Load from the Hub
docs.text: Models are saved in the Hugging Face format. After import timber, AutoModel.from_pretrained loads a model from the Hub or from a folder.
